extracted.intended_audience: scholars and students of media sociology, communication researchers, journalism scholars
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and applies criteria for how news is produced and judged in journalistic organizations (newsworthiness, organizational routines, source/audience influences) based on Herbert Gans' Deciding What's News and its evaluation. Useful for analyzing or designing studies of news production and for normative reform proposals (e.g., multiperspectivism).

rubrics_metrics.name: Newsworthiness / Story "suitability" considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories become important by satisfying one consideration and increase in importance with every additional one they satisfy (additive model). These considerations include rank in government and other hierarchies, impact on the country, impact on many people, and significance for the past and future.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gans treats news value as additive. Reporters like novelty (but not too novel); editors favor stories already “certified” by acceptance elsewhere; prediction is avoided as risky. Use these considerations to assess whether a story will be selected; the more considerations satisfied, the higher its newsworthiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additive model of news value (general heuristic)
rubrics_metrics.description: News value is measured as an additive set of considerations — a story’s importance grows as it satisfies more relevant considerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply multiple small, easily-applied checks rather than single grand criteria. This heuristic favors stories that are flexible to rationalize, quick to apply, and efficient to produce; it also explains conformity across outlets when the same considerations are used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for certified/validated stories (inter-media confirmation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors favor news that has already been “certified” by acceptance elsewhere (the practice of looking to other media for confirmation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The dependence on peer outlets (especially The New York Times) as an arbiter reduces risk and uncertainty; competitive pressures and inter-media confirmation explain why outlets converge on the same stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of prediction in reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists and editors tend to steer clear of prediction because it is risky and potentially damaging to credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid making forward-looking assertions or forecasts in news coverage unless highly certain; this is treated as an anti-pattern for routine news judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source power and source-orientation
rubrics_metrics.description: Sources (especially powerful public officials) play the primary role in shaping news; journalists depend on sources and often act as intermediaries between sources and editors/audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Powerful sources are economical to cover (easy access, known locations); non-elites typically enter coverage only via disruption or violation of order. Treat the ‘‘source landscape’’ as a primary explanatory variable for coverage patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tug-of-war between sources and audiences (reporter vs editor orientation)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a continuing tension: reporters are more source-oriented while editors are more conscious of what will appeal to audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the differing incentives within news organizations: reporters pitch stories to editors (seller-buyer negotiation), editors weigh audience appeal. This affects story selection, framing, and emphasis; systematic audience research is often underused or viewed suspiciously by journalists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited knowledge of and distance from audiences
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists often have little direct knowledge of their audiences and may be leery of systematic audience research; they tend to write for people close to them professionally/socially and see themselves as proxies for the average audience member.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating news decisions, account for this proximal social orientation and the resulting blind spots regarding broader audience perspectives; reliance on proxy judgments can perpetuate narrow coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizational routines and bureaucratic determinants
rubrics_metrics.description: Newsmaking is shaped by organizational objectives, bureaucratic structures, routines, and professional values — e.g., seniority, striving for promotion, routinization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat news as an organizational product; routines (deadlines, beats, hierarchy) constrain choices and favor efficiency. Organizational design choices (division of labor, recruitment) embed controls on content even absent overt censorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Efficiency and uncertainty-reduction as decision criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Considerations used in story selection must be immediately applicable, help avoid excessive uncertainty, be flexible and easily rationalized to others, and be efficient (guarantee best results for least effort).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These practical constraints explain journalists’ reliance on heuristics and on established sources/frames; they also produce pressures toward conformity and make media susceptible to outside influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embedded professional values and paraideology
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalistic values are embedded in the profession and organizational setting (paraideology) rather than located solely in individuals; Gans locates the news as roughly right-liberal or left-conservative and nearer to Progressive traditions (valuing reform, meritocracy, anti-bigness, craftsmanship over technology).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Infer normative orientations from aggregated content and routines rather than attributing bias to isolated reporters; acknowledge that professed detachment coexists with implicit shared values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation and inclusion criteria (who gets covered)
rubrics_metrics.description: Most news covers the affluent and established elites; non-elites appear mainly through protest, scandal, or disruption. Known actors receive most coverage; unknowns get a smaller share.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this criterion to evaluate representativeness: ask whether coverage broadens the symbolic arena to include bottom-up impacts and under-reported perspectives. Recognize structural filters that favor elites and routine actors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normative reform: multiperspectivism and diversification of sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Gans recommends broadening news to include more national coverage beyond federal government, more bottom-up views on event impacts, more representative news, and diversification of sources and perspectives (multiperspectivism).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy or institutional remedies include independent monitors of journalistic performance, publicizing studies, and proposals like an Endowment for News to subsidize underrepresented perspectives; ideological studies are acceptable if values are explicit.

rubrics_metrics.name: News as packaging/marketable product (market orientation)
rubrics_metrics.description: News production is the process of packaging the daily flow of events into a marketable product for audiences; journalists solve packaging problems under economic constraints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate stories in light of marketability pressures: constraints often determine what is covered more than abstract normative ideals; note that neither journalists nor business departments necessarily know how to expand audience size.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of competition in breaking automatic application of considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Competitive factors (looking to each other for confirmation) demonstrate that newsworthiness considerations are not mechanically applied; outlets monitor peers for validation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for market competition and imitation when diagnosing convergence in coverage; the existence of an arbiter outlet (e.g., NYT) amplifies conformity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fieldwork/participant observation methodological standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Participant observation is necessary to observe behavior itself (not just reports of behavior); media fieldwork is time-consuming and imposes researcher adaptation to the studied community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For research or evaluation of newswork, prioritize naturalistic, in-situ observation when possible to capture routines, negotiations, and tacit norms; be mindful of the intensive labor and organizational embedment required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caveat on case-study generalizability (external validity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Findings from a few deeply-studied organizations (networks, newsmagazines) are tentative and impressionistic; external validity is limited and the special mission of studied media (celebratory, national-voice roles) affects generalization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply conclusions cautiously to other media forms (newspapers, online outlets) and changed historical contexts; explicitly consider whether institutional missions bias observed patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural control and rare explicit censorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicit, overt acts of censorship by outside actors are rare, but control over content is built into organizational processes (recruitment patterns, norms, occasional top-executive vetoes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing autonomy, distinguish between overt censorship episodes and the routine structural constraints that shape what is feasible to cover; look for how suggestions are transmitted or neutralized via division of labor.

rubrics_metrics.name: News functions: managing the symbolic arena and latent societal functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Among its functions, news manages the symbolic arena — making nation, societal, and other messages available — and serves latent functions like testing leaders, supplying political feedback, acting as moral guardian and agent of social control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as a lens for evaluating news content’s social role: examine how coverage constructs nationhood, legitimates social hierarchies, and frames public rituals; consider latent consequences beyond manifest reporting.
